Subject: Re: Winterizing Sea Wren — what to buy, and in what order

Dana — you're right to want to understand your own boat. Two or three hours with a helper is a realistic number, and $465 isn't a ripoff; that's about what the antifreeze and the shop's time run. Here's the order.

One correction first, and gently: green automotive antifreeze is ethylene glycol. It's toxic, it isn't rated for your raw water system, and it ends up in the bay. The raw side and the domestic water side want pink propylene glycol RV/marine antifreeze. No harm meant toward Hector — his boat's come through the cold fine, but that's not the manufacturer spec, and green is what we don't want in the water.

What to buy:
- Pink propylene glycol RV/marine antifreeze. About 2 gallons for the engine's raw water side, 2–3 more for the domestic water system. Those are estimates only, so buy enough to complete the manufacturer winterizing procedures, then verify the protection at the end.
- A coolant hydrometer. The 3GM30F is freshwater cooled with a heat exchanger, two sides. The engine coolant side just needs a strength check — 50/50 is good to about -20°F. The raw water side is the one that freezes and cracks things.

Order of work:
1. Warm engine first. Change oil and filter while it's warm, top off the fuel tank, add stabilizer, and run it about 10 minutes to get the additive through.
2. Before you start the engine, set up exhaust collection. Raw water discharge comes out through the exhaust and all of it gets captured for proper disposal — not into the river, not a drop. Have a helper watching flow and collection.
3. Water heater: the bypass valve is behind the companionway steps on the Catalina. Switch off the water heater breaker before you drain, and leave it off until it's refilled in spring. Drain the tank first or you'll waste six gallons of pink.
4. Raw water side: seacock closed, strainer feeding antifreeze to the pump at idle. Keep the pump wet, don't run it dry, shut down when it's done, and leave the seacock closed.
5. Collect the domestic water system discharge too, same as the raw side.

Check the discharged mixture for the required winter protection. Pink color isn't a test.

Keep a spare impeller aboard — cheap insurance. Pull the old one out and look at it while you're in there, and don't run the raw pump dry doing it.

Why this order matters: we had a hard Christmas freeze a few years back and three boats on C dock cracked exhaust elbows or strainers. Every one of them had skipped or rushed the raw water side. That side is what freezes and fails; the coolant side is just a hydrometer reading.

If you want, I'll come down to the boat Saturday morning and be your second set of hands. That makes it an afternoon instead of a project.
